Entries are Paul's own annotations paraphrased, and citations are recorded as he wrote them; I did not verify them externally.

Overarching argument: the section extends the static influence-maximization entries (Kempe et al. 2003; Nemhauser-Wolsey-Fisher 1978, covered elsewhere) into a dynamic regime organized in three tiers that mirror the Melange architecture. Tier 1 is one-shot greedy, which is static and submodular and gives the 1-1/e (about 63%) bound. Tier 2 is adaptive greedy, the bridge: a subordinate routine that replans within a campaign as intelligence arrives, with a survival guarantee (Golovin-Krause; CELF makes it computationally practical). Tier 3 is the RL envelope, where a learned outer policy handles cross-campaign compounding, where no greedy guarantee reaches.

Unifying claim: the inner static problem is submodular, the inner sequential problem is adaptive submodular, and the full cross-campaign problem is non-submodular. Paul asserts that RL4CCIM confirms the last point for complex contagion, and that the non-submodular regime is where the durable competitive moat lives.

Systems linked: the operational layer (D* Lite / LPA*, incremental replanning) maps to adaptive submodularity; the strategic layer (MCTS and the orienteering "reach-while-collecting" frame) maps to the RL-IM sequential, long-horizon problem; the political-capital budget maps to GCOMB's budget constraint; the subordinate greedy routine feeds the outer MDP through marginal-influence shaping rewards.

Research questions and implicit hypotheses: (a) whether coalition formation in Congress is a complex contagion (a fence-sitter commits only once enough allies have), which Paul calls "plausibly" true and which would place Melange outside the submodular regime; (b) whether relationship and persuasion costs, unknown a priori, can be learned by probing (Kamarthi); (c) whether lobbying commitment that is probabilistic rather than guaranteed (Chen 2021) changes the seeding policy.

Stated gaps and caveats in the addendum: adaptive submodularity presumes exact expected spread, which is NP-hard in general, and this is the stated reason Paul still drifts toward learned methods. The frontier paragraph says the four anchored RL entries are "sufficient"; the section in fact anchors seven RL-IM entries plus foundations, so that sentence is loosely worded. The frontier work (MaDGNN) is named without authors or DOI and is not anchored. The Golovin entry's "first to study influence maximization under the adaptive model" is Paul's priority claim and is unverified here.

Overarching argument: Paul asks whether an industry's year-over-year economic performance predicts its federal political spending (campaign contributions and lobbying), and whether expected partisan control of Congress shapes the amount and partisan direction of that spending. Five initial sectors: commercial banks, credit unions, life insurance, auto manufacturing, crypto (crypto analyzed separately). Hypotheses: H1 deep pockets (positive growth effect); H1-alt distress (negative or asymmetric effect); H2 access-seeking (Republican share rises with expected Republican control); H3 stakes (total contributions rise with a toss-up); H4 lobbying tracks current control more than projected control.

Design synthesis: one distributed-lag model with prior-year and same-year growth (prior-year is the main test, for reverse-causality and timing reasons); pooled panel with sector fixed effects; log CPI-deflated dollars; within-sector z-scored growth; negative-growth indicator; lagged lobbying as a control (cites Kerr, Lincoln & Mishra 2014); projected control as probability of majority (Shift = P minus current majority; Tossup = 1 minus |2P minus 1|), with a directional RShare outcome; year fixed effects as the robustness alternative; wild cluster bootstrap for p-values with 5 clusters and Driscoll-Kraay SEs where year-level terms appear. Scope finding: this document is an engineering plan for the Melange staffer social network, not an annotated literature review. It cites no scholarly works, papers, books or authors. The only external "sources" are data providers and documents (House Statement of Disbursements, Senate Report of the Secretary / GPO Serial Set, LDA API at lda.gov, Politico Pro directory, LittleSis, legislators-historical, LegiStorm, ProPublica disbursements mirror). Overarching arguments and design rulings:
- Layering: the member layer (cosponsorship and press) stays independent. The staffer network is its own layer below members, with members as attachment points and no member-member edges. Lobbyists enter as outsiders via revolving-door edges. Layers combine only at analysis time in a multiplex, never inside each other's weights. Multiplying the cosponsorship adjacency into staffer weights is banned as double-counting and as a comparability contaminant (same failure class as the LD-2 circularity).
- Edge rule (OVERLAP): a person-person edge requires real temporal overlap in the same container, weighted by overlap duration times container kappa. Sequence across offices is a trajectory property (ordered stints, office-to-office moves), never a person-person edge. Every build must emit a negative control counting edges a build without the overlap test would produce.
- Education is excluded (weight alpha=0 kept in code), so the final weight reduces to W = w_work, purely staffer-derived and therefore comparable to the bill graph.
- Non-circularity: LobbyView network.csv, lobbyview_network_member.csv, our_network_*.csv and bill_lobbying_sidecar.json are banned as circular. LD-2 filings never name members, so lobbied-member edges are joins by construction; zero influence or predictor phrasing on LDA-derived edges is a language law (I-15). Revolving-layer join on lda_source_person_id verified not circular.
- Inference is never merged with observation: predicted destinations live in a separate exploratory tier, to avoid self-confirmation.
- Identity: STRICT-BIOGUIDE (no fuzzy member joins), declaration-directed matching, paired control arms per widening tier with a positive control, and coverage alarms with match-rate floors that abort fail-closed.

- Whether committee payrolls (missed by a prior parse, "committee membership does not exist on disk" was wrong) are the main source of cross-party ties, since personal offices are partisan silos. Committee kappa is treated as load-bearing for whole-graph connectivity; the plan asks whether committees are what hold the graph together.
- Side (maj/min/bipartisan/unknown) is four-valued because committee staff are mixed; the kappa=0.40 opposite-side row is reachable, not structurally dead.
- Centrality is computed per connected component, since eigenvector centrality is ill-defined on fragmented graphs and PARTIAL_NULL at L3/L4 is read as fragmentation, not iteration limits.
- Interval algebra: union before intersection, because naive pairwise summation invents about 13.7M co-tenure days (1.0%).

G-9 (the I-4 gold set, 200 identity and 100 parser samples carry proposed decisions, not human labels) blocks all arming. G-6 (everything but payroll undated) is the largest effort. works.title: Strategic and Sequential Links between Campaign Donations and Lobbying
works.summary:
Kim, Stuckatz and Wolters link LDA bill mentions to FEC donations for U.S. public manufacturing firms (2,703 firms, 979 members of Congress, 2008-2017, 16.4M firm-politician-year rows). They test whether a donation comes before lobbying on bills that the recipient sponsored, cosponsored or handled in committee. In the descriptive 2013 snapshot, only 519 of 11,829 public firms both donated and lobbied, and they account for about 85% of the money. Under firm-politician fixed effects, a first-time donation (no gift in the prior 3 years) goes with a 10-12 point higher chance of lobbying a related bill in the same year, against a base rate of about 0.05. Matched difference-in-differences gives about 8.5 points at year t (Senate), falling to about 3 points by t+3. The effect is concentrated in committee-related lobbying and is largest for corporate PACs. The authors read this as access-buying timing, not quid pro quo.

For Paul's systems, the paper matters mainly because its estimand differs from what the system measured. The FEC-to-LDA bridge (round 3) is a cross-sectional member-by-industry-by-cycle rank correlation. It is dominated by trade associations, credits only sponsors and cosponsors, and controls for finance-committee seats. Its four-control partial of about 0 does not contradict a within-pair, onset-timed, committee-driven effect among public firms. The bridge design actually controls away the channel Kim finds strongest. The paper also cuts against the system's "FEC leads LDA by 42 months" heuristic: its effect is concurrent and gone within two to three years.

The paper also builds its outcome from the same bill-roster join that the system ruled circular. It escapes circularity only because its treatment, the donation, is timed independently of the join. Its identity work (gvkey matching, constrained graph clustering, hand-coded validation) is a method source for Mentat's donor ladder. Every figure here is the paper's own; none has been reproduced locally (UNVERIFIED per DE-062).
works.question: Are campaign donations and lobbying activity linked for the same interest group-politician pair, and do donations precede lobbying on bills tied to the donee's committee seats, sponsorship or co-sponsorship (the "access-buying" hypothesis)?
works.method: Step 1: descriptive tables and cross-sectional log-log fits (Table 2, Fig 2, Appendix C and E). Step 2: linear probability models with firm, year, politician and firm-politician fixed effects, with controls for party, majority status, committee chair and powerful-committee membership (Table 3, Table F.1; standard errors clustered by firm). Step 3: difference-in-differences combined with matching (Imai, Kim and Wang 2020). Treated pairs are first-time donors defined over L = 3 years. Matched controls are other firms with no donation to the same politician in t to t-3. Matching uses Mahalanobis distance on sales, employees and pre-treatment lobbying, with 10 closest comparators. The DiD estimator (Eq. 4) differences outcome changes between t-1 and t+F for treated pairs versus the matched mean, averaged over pairs. Confidence intervals come from a block bootstrap. Outcome: Y=1 if the firm lobbies a bill that is sponsored, co-sponsored, or assigned to a committee on which the politician serves (each measured separately).

findings.finding: Descriptive 2013 snapshot: only 519 of 11,829 public companies (about 4%) both donated and lobbied, yet they account for most money in politics.
Firm-politician dyads with both donations and bill-related lobbying are extremely rare but carry large money: 13,886 dyads out of 6,541,437 possible.
findings.location: Sec 2.1, printed p. 13 (PDF p. 15), Table 2 right panel
findings.numbers: 13,886 dyads (<0.1% of all possible); more than $520 million, 17% of 2013 spending; 15,420 donation-only dyads, 13,078 of them from employee donations

findings.finding: Firm-level corporate PAC donations and lobbying spending are positively related for firms doing both.
findings.numbers: Log-log slope beta = 0.88, adjusted R2 about 0.4; text says a 10% PAC increase goes with 8.8% more lobbying, while the Fig 2 caption computes 8.7%

findings.finding: Other donation types show the same firm-level pattern (all donations, executives, employees, government relations).
findings.numbers: beta 0.58 (R2 0.29) all donations; 0.58 (0.17) executives; 0.68 (0.23) employees; 0.78 (0.20) government relations; years 2000-2017

findings.finding: Within firm-politician pairs, a firm's first-time donation raises the probability it lobbies a bill tied to that politician in the same year.
findings.numbers: Donation coefficient 0.102-0.118 (SEs about 0.008-0.009), N = 16,428,834. Firm-politician and year FE (last column) gives 0.118. Baseline probability about 0.05; sponsors 0.002, co-sponsors 0.026, committee members 0.043

works.title: Measuring the dynamical evolution of the United States lobbying network
works.summary:
Bacik, Ondras, Rudkin, Dunkel and Kim build a yearly five-layer directed network from LobbyView, which is derived from LDA LD-2 filings. The layers are clients, registrants (K-Street firms and in-house departments), lobbyists, government entities and legislators. The analyzed sample is 1,277,411 filings from 1999 to 2023. The work is descriptive network physics, not causal inference. Its main findings: 200-500 K-Street registrants enter and leave each year, and only 20% of the firms active in 2000 were still active in 2020. Up to one-third of client-registrant ties are rewired each year. Attachment is linearly preferential, which gives a heavy-tailed distribution of clients per firm (exponent about 1.5, cutoff about 86). Money is concentrated: the cumulative Gini is about 0.8 for clients and firms. Agency-target portfolios form blocks by presidential administration. Senate cross-party cosponsorship fell about 40% while lobbyist bipartisanship did not fall. A single SOPA case (Q4 2011, 67 public firms) shows the IT sector over-represented, with P(IT | SOPA) above 0.4 against a base rate of about 0.1.

For Paul's systems the paper matters mostly through what LDA data cannot show. Legislators enter the paper's network only through lobbyists' one-time disclosures of past covered positions. Those disclosures have no dates, and the LDA never records registrant-legislator contact. That independently supports the system's refutation of the lobbied-member link and its fail-closed handling of contacts and identities. The paper's 40% NAICS coverage supports the rule that client names decide classification. Its K-Street versus in-house distinction supports Mentat's rule of never adding hired-firm and in-house lobbying. Its "election synchronization" finding is about which agencies are targeted, not about money, so it does not support a phase effect on lobbying dollars. The paper contains no press or sentiment data.
works.question: How does the US federal lobbying network (clients, registrants, lobbyists, government entities, legislators) evolve over time? Specifically: (a) what growth and attachment rules govern client-registrant ties; (b) how does the network adapt to crises and to election or administration cycles; (c) can LDA disclosure data support probabilistic analysis of lobbying pathways for individual bills, issues, or firms, demonstrated on the Stop Online Piracy Act (SOPA, 2011).
works.method: Descriptive and empirical statistics on a time-indexed multilayer directed graph. Steps: (1) in- and out-degree CCDFs by layer; MLE fits of an augmented power law with exponential cutoff, a log-normal and a Weibull, with the power law preferred (Fig 2F, SI Fig S11). (2) Preferential attachment: attachment and detachment functions by registrant in-degree, cumulated, with linearity tested (Fig 2E, SI VIII.B). (3) Survival or retention probability by year and age-conditioned exit (SI VIII.A). (4) Pareto charts and Gini indices of monetary flow (SI V). (5) Issue and target portfolios: client-share matrices, year-to-year Spearman correlation, PCA (SI XI). (6) Bipartite clustering coefficients and largest connected component, against a configuration-model null (SI IX). (7) SOPA pathway probabilities: uniform client draw, conditional probability shift Delta P(sector | SOPA) (Fig 4, SI XII). (8) Polarization: bipartisan cosponsorship index, lobbyist bipartisan index, modularity (SI XIII).

works.title: Empirical Models of Lobbying
works.summary:
Bombardini and Trebbi (2020) is a narrative review of empirical lobbying research. It contains no new estimation. It sorts the literature into quid pro quo models, where political resources are exchanged for policy, and informational models, where interest groups pass expertise to less-informed policymakers. It then asks how each line of work identifies policy supply and demand and the counterfactual of no lobbying.

The review reaches three conclusions that matter for Paul's systems.

First, structural estimates of what money buys are fragile. Kang (2016) estimates that lobbying raises enactment by only 0.021% to 0.415% over an 8% baseline (538 energy policies, 110th Congress), yet the same model implies more than $500m of value per policy. A naive Farm Bill comparison gives a return near 600,000% ($22bn of 2000 subsidies against under $3.7m of agribusiness PAC money). The authors read these figures as symptoms of misspecification or of influence channels left out of the model. Adding an electoral-vote channel (Bombardini and Trebbi 2011) brings implied returns down to plausible levels.

Second, lobbying is persistent: 92% of firms that lobby in one year lobby the next (Kerr et al. 2014). The structure of the industry has also shifted: from 1999 to 2008 the in-house share of lobbying fell from about 60% to under 40%, while external lobbying doubled.

Third, in the revolving-door literature, a lobbyist's revenue depends on the patron staying in office. Former aides lose a persistent 24% of revenue when their senator exits (Blanes i Vidal et al. 2012), and lobbyists follow politicians across committee reassignments (Bertrand et al. 2014).

For the system as built, the review supports keeping money a minority, saturating channel in the flip and money-response engines, and treating ROI figures as fragile. It supports the persistence-based lobbying nowcast in Mentat and the rule that in-house and outside-firm lobbying are never summed. It also exposes one gap: the staffer route costs decay with time since overlap but do not account for whether the anchoring member is still in office or holds a powerful committee seat.
works.question: Is lobbying (direct or intermediated business-government interaction over policy) welfare-enhancing or welfare-distorting? The review organizes recent empirical work on quid pro quo and informational lobbying, asks how to identify policy supply and demand and the counterfactual equilibrium with no lobbying, and assesses how distorted equilibrium policy is relative to the social optimum.
works.method: Narrative review organized as quid pro quo (structural econometric and reduced-form) versus informational. Structural methods reviewed: Kang (2016) Tullock-contest game with simulated maximum likelihood and equilibrium selection; Bombardini and Trebbi (2011) structural first-order conditions yielding a dollar-per-vote cost; Huneeus and Kim (2019) heterogeneous-firm general-equilibrium model estimated by minimum distance on simulated moments. Reduced-form methods reviewed: difference-in-differences (Blanes i Vidal et al. 2012), instrumental variables (de Figueiredo and Silverman 2006 with overhead rates; Goldstein and You 2017 with distance to Washington), natural experiments (Kerr et al. 2014 H-1B cap; Dellavigna et al. 2016 Berlusconi advertising), and observational contact and mobility regressions (Bertrand et al. 2014; Hirsch et al. 2019). Text methods: NLP to classify bill policies (Kang 2016, p.397) and latent semantic analysis of comments (Bertrand et al. 2018a, p.408, n.35).

findings.finding: Survey context: 53% of respondents called lobbyists and special interest groups in Washington a very big problem, versus 38% for illegal immigration (Pew surveys, Sept 2018-Mar 2019).
Kang (2016) energy-sector lobbying: only 8% of 538 policies in 445 bills are enacted; policies with no lobbying are enacted about 1% of the time; policies with two or more lobbying players about 24%.
findings.numbers: 8% overall; 1% no lobbying; 24% two or more lobbyists

findings.finding: Kang's model implies lobbying raises enactment by only 0.021% to 0.415% over an 8% baseline, and average returns to lobbying of 137% (renewables) to 152% (oil and gas). The implied monetary value per policy above $500 million is flagged by the authors as possibly signaling misspecification.
findings.numbers: 0.021%-0.415% effect; 137%-152% returns; >$500m per policy

findings.finding: Bombardini and Trebbi (2011) structural bargaining model on Congressional campaign contributions estimates $200-$400 of donations per vote acquired and a precise average rate of return on political spending. Adding the electoral-vote channel makes implied returns far more reasonable.
findings.numbers: $200-$400 per vote; agriculture return about $13.7 per dollar at the margin; simulated returns 10%-20% per year

findings.finding: Farm Bill comparison: about $22 billion in 2000 agribusiness subsidies against under $3.7 million in agribusiness PAC contributions implies a naive return of about 600,000%, which the authors argue shows that observable contributions miss other influence channels.

Huneeus and Kim (2019): a 10% increase in lobbying raises revenue 3%. Federal lobbying reduces aggregate US productivity 22%, with 59% from misallocation to lobbying (less productive) firms and 41% from missing entry of productive firms.

The review cites Kim (2018) LobbyView as the state-of-the-art Compustat-linked lobbying data set used by Huneeus and Kim.
Both separate lobbying from PAC money; the review puts total lobbying at $3-3.5bn a year against $200-250m in yearly PAC donations.
The review's account of money as access with small measured policy effects is consistent with Kalla and Broockman's evidence that contributions buy access.
Kang's mapping of lobbying to provision-level policies required extensive NLP preanalysis; position extraction from lobbying reports addresses the same problem.
The review's access-versus-expertise evidence (Bertrand et al. 2014) bears on which lobbying skills are teachable.
The review uses DIME campaign-finance ideology scores, citing Bonica (2016) DIME database rather than this 2013 paper; same scoring lineage.
Both treat donations and lobbying as linked instruments; the review stresses multiple influence tools used simultaneously with substitution patterns (Bombardini and Trebbi 2011).
Both relate firm lobbying to firm size, the stylized fact the review reports from Huneeus and Kim.

works.title: An Application of Data Mining Techniques to Explore Congressional Lobbying Records for Patterns in Pediatric Special Interest Expenditures Prior to the Affordable Care Act
works.summary:
Harrison, Dreisbach, Basit and Keim-Malpass (2018) is a short data report, not a study of influence. It parses one quarter of Senate LDA XML (Q4 2009, just before the ACA) into eight pandas data frames. It sums reported dollars by umbrella issue code (Taxation $527.1M, Health $436.7M, with no denominator for the filing count) and finds 35 records whose Specific Issues text contains "pediatric". It runs no statistics. Its useful content is a list of data hazards:
- **Two series mixed:** the XML amount field does not separate in-house expenditures from outside-firm income.
- **Imprecise amounts:** expenses under $5,000 appear only as a checkbox, and income is rounded to the nearest $10,000.
- **Bundled issues:** one filing lists many issues, so dollars cannot be assigned to a single issue.
- **Filing time vs activity time:** files are grouped by when they were filed, so a quarter's files can carry activity from 2002 to 2008.

For Paul's systems, those hazards matter more than the results. Mentat's lobbying card and `sector_spend.py` now enforce the paper's main warning. They keep outside-firm fees and in-house expenses as two series and never add them (D-064, commit 914623152, which removed a double-counted $139.4M telecom total on 2026-10-09). `sector_spend.py` also assigns filings by activity period and keeps only the latest amendment.

The older LobbyView collector does not follow the same rule. Its per-side `amount_sum` and its top-spender `total_amount` add self-filer expenses and hired-firm income together. The brain's "ABA $228M vs CUNA $93M" figure probably comes from that mixed sum (UNVERIFIED). On issue codes, the collector correctly counts reports rather than dollars, which avoids the bundling trap that inflates the paper's own per-code dollar totals. The paper has nothing to say about networks, persuasion, legislators or elections.
works.question: Stated in Sec. 1 and Sec. 2: the paper illustrates data parsing principles for mining federal lobbying records, and shows how one might investigate trends in how pediatric health concerns enter the political environment, using Q4 2009 LDA filings made before the Affordable Care Act. No formal hypothesis is stated.
works.method: Descriptive data engineering in Python 3.6.4: ElementTree parses the XML hierarchy; os.listdir enumerates files; a parsing loop (pseudocode in Fig. 2) converts records into Pandas data frames, with defaultdict holding a master dictionary (Sec. 2.2-2.3). Filing and Issue frames are merged, and reported dollar amounts are summed by issue code (a Pandas series grouped by code, Sec. 2.3). A search function returns every record whose Specific Issues text contains a user-supplied term; the term "pediatric" is used (Sec. 2.4). Search hits are compared with the code-level totals (Sec. 2.4). No statistical tests, models or regressions are run.

Health Issues is the second-largest umbrella code by reported dollars.
The pediatric keyword search returns 35 records from the Q4 2009 frame, spread across several umbrella codes.
findings.numbers: 35 hits; codes include Health Issues, Budget Appropriations, Science/Technology, Education, Disaster Planning & Emergencies, Medicare/Medicaid

findings.finding: Pediatric-related issues are bundled with many unrelated issues inside single filings, so dollars spent on pediatric lobbying cannot be isolated.
findings.numbers: not quantified; illustrated with one filing listing multiple vaccine, Medicare/Medicaid, FDA and pandemic issues together

findings.finding: Records are grouped by filing date, so a quarter's files include activity from earlier years.
findings.numbers: activity dated 2002-2008 filed in Q4 2009; a date filter restricts output to 2009 events

findings.numbers: not quantified

It does the text analysis Harrison proposes as future work (Sec. 4), labelling bill positions from LDA report text for 2009-2022.
Both use LDA LD-2 filings; Bacik builds yearly multilayer networks over 1999-2023 from LobbyView, which Harrison's one-quarter parse never reaches.
Furnas uses CRP-curated LDA lobbying expenditures, so the expense-vs-income semantics Harrison flags bear on its lobbying totals.
Paul's report draws on LDA disclosures, so the same caution about mixing the two series and about rounding applies.

works.title: The partisan ties of lobbying firms
works.summary:
Furnas, Heaney and LaPira (2019) ask whether US contract lobbying firms have stable partisan identities and whether ties to the majority party raise their revenue. The sample is 1,603 LDA contract registrants observed by quarter from 2008 Q1 to 2016 Q3 (33,243 firm-quarters). A firm's partisanship comes from the share of its lobbyists' FEC contributions that go to one party, using cutoffs of 85, 90 or 95%. These identities are reliable (Fleiss kappa 0.84 to 0.86). Between 42% and 60% of firms are partisan, and bipartisan firms earn the highest average revenue.

The outcome is real revenue per lobbyist per quarter, with a mean of $74k. In all six levels models, alignment with the House majority adds about $5,000 to $6,000 per lobbyist per quarter. Senate alignment matters only under the time-fixed measure. A kernel-weighted difference-in-differences around the 2011 House flip finds that Republican-aligned firms gained just over $10k over the year while Democratic-aligned firms lost more than $40k. The 2015 Senate flip shows no significant effect. Across all tests, House ties support the revenue hypothesis in 12 of 13 and Senate ties in 3 of 13.

For Paul's systems, the main relevance is to the Mentat sector-growth and lobbying-forecast lanes, not to the Melange engine. The study supports keeping House and Senate separate and expecting a weaker Senate signal. It measures a premium clients are willing to pay for perceived access to the majority. That is a market valuation: it is not a measure of persuasion and not an access probability. The effect is also distributional: control changes move revenue between partisan firms. The paper does not estimate how sector totals respond, which is the level Mentat's lobbying model works at. This reading is UNVERIFIED agent analysis until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
works.question: Do partisan ties between US lobbying firms and the partisan leadership of Congress raise the revenue those firms earn from clients? Are lobbying firms institutions with relatively stable partisan identities, and do ties to House and Senate majorities return different amounts (abstract; pp.1-2)?
works.method: Two sets of linear panel models. Set 1 (levels, Table 2, models 1.1-1.6): revenue per lobbyist regressed on House alignment and Senate alignment, crossed as time-fixed vs time-varying partisanship and 85%, 90% and 95% giving thresholds, plus controls (number of clients, client diversity = Simpson reciprocal diversity of issues plus industries, law firm, international office, domestic offices, firm age). Firm random effects, year fixed effects, HC3 Arellano standard errors clustered by firm. H2 tested with a restricted F-test that the House and Senate coefficients are equal. Set 2 (first differences, Table 3, models 2.1-2.6): change in revenue on change in alignment, clients and diversity. Partisan measure: a firm is aligned with a chamber's leadership party if its lobbyists' contributions exceed the threshold share to that party; bipartisan or unclear firms are coded as aligned with neither chamber (p.3). Reliability: Fleiss kappa 0.86 (time-fixed) and 0.84 (time-varying). Validity: correlations of 0.31 to 0.55 between contribution-based partisanship and founder-based partisanship (web pages); time-fixed vs time-varying correlation 0.62 to 0.63 (p.3). Causal test: kernel-weighted difference-in-differences (Hazlett 2019) around the 2011 and 2015 takeovers (p.7-8).

findings.finding: Partisan identities of lobbying firms are relatively stable and reliable (kappa and time-fixed/time-varying correlation); founder-based partisanship correlates with contribution-based partisanship.
findings.numbers: Fleiss kappa 0.86 time-fixed, 0.84 time-varying; correlations 0.62-0.63 across measures; founder correlations 0.31-0.55 (p<=0.05)

findings.numbers: 42-60% partisan; 40-58% bipartisan; 84% of firms had nonzero giving

findings.finding: Bipartisan firms consistently earned more average revenue than partisan-leaning firms; Democratic and Republican firms were at rough parity, with a small advantage that shifted with congressional control; unclassified firms earned least.
findings.numbers: No point estimates in text; Democratic firms led 2008-2010, Republican firms 2011-2016

findings.finding: House partisan alignment is significantly and positively associated with firm revenue in all six panel models (H1 supported for the House).
findings.numbers: Time-fixed coefficients 5,536 (SE 1,734), 6,527 (1,944), 6,096 (2,132); time-varying 5,148 (1,298), 5,346 (1,343), 4,940 (1,396); all p<=0.05. Text: about US$5,000-6,000 per lobbyist per quarter

The restricted test of equal House and Senate effects (H2) is significant only with time-varying measures.
findings.numbers: Time-fixed F = 4, 3, 1 (n.s.); time-varying F = 20*, 23*, 24* (df 1, 33,200)

related.why: Bacik reports that registrants employing lobbyists with connections to both parties generate higher income per lobbyist (Fig. S46C) while legislators polarize; this paper finds bipartisan lobbying firms earn the highest average revenue.

Same first author; reports minimal overlap between organizations that lobby and those that make campaign expenditures, which explains why a lobbying-revenue premium need not appear in PAC giving-share tests.
Both build on Lobbying Disclosure Act filings; this paper uses the registrant-versus-client split to isolate contract firms.
Both infer the partisanship or ideology of actors from campaign contribution records.
Kim links campaign donations and lobbying sequentially; this paper uses lobbyists' donations as a partisan identity signal for firms.
The review discusses Bertrand et al. (2014) on connections versus expertise, which this paper extends from individual lobbyists to firms.

works.title: Learnable Skills, or Unteachable Instinct? What Can and What Cannot Be Taught in the Lobbying Profession
works.summary:
Holyoke, Brown and LaPira write a conceptual essay with a curriculum proposal. It is not an empirical study. They argue that most of lobbying can be taught at graduate level, in three areas: knowledge (process, policy and analytics), communication and messaging, and relationship building. Relationship building is only partly teachable because it depends on personality. The paper has no data, sample, window or tests. Every number it gives comes from someone else: about 30,000 DC lobbyists in 2012, 12% of them under 35 (Rehr 2012); 52% came through the revolving door (LaPira and Thomas 2014); 37% knew next to nothing about LDA/HLOGA. Its substantive claims are hedged with words like "arguably" and "suggests". They are: relationships rest on mutual need and are aimed at lawmakers with a relevant constituency stake, not on friendship; group members contact lawmakers more than non-members do; identical mass messages are worthless; campaign finance matters less than people think, and few lobbyists give at all.

The paper is weak evidence for Paul's systems. It is useful as framing, not calibration. Its sharpest bearing is on the staffer overlap router. In the code (`fec/surfaces/staffer_overlap_routes.py:33-39`), tie strength is proximity × log2(1 + shared days / 30) of dated co-work. The paper says a working relationship comes from mutual need and targeting, not from time spent in the same office. So the router's strength is at best a proxy for the chance of contact. Treat it as a heuristic cost, never as relationship strength or access (D-025). The paper also loosely backs three things: the flip model treating money as the minor channel; Terrier's Sphere of Influence using civic engagement; and the footprint version of Demographic Potential, through constituency-stake targeting. None of these backs any weight or constant.
works.question: Can the knowledge, skills and abilities needed for lobbying be taught to pre- and early-career lobbyists at the graduate professional level, and which parts cannot be taught (Executive Summary p.2; "What Can Be Taught" pp.8-19)?
works.method: Qualitative and argumentative. Literature synthesis from political science on interest groups and lobbying, interview-informed claims, and personal experience, used to propose a graduate curriculum (seminars, simulations, capstone, internship or practicum). No statistical estimation, coding, or formal test of the proposed curriculum.

findings.finding: Central claim: much of lobbying, though not all, can be taught at graduate level. Three areas are proposed: knowledge (process, policy, analytic), communication and messaging, and relationship building.
findings.location: Executive Summary p.2; What Can Be Taught pp.8-19
findings.numbers: None

findings.finding: Experience and personality limit what training can do; the authors argue good instincts are as much a product of training as of experience or natural ability.
findings.numbers: None

findings.finding: Lobbyist population and career entry: of roughly 30,000 people who more or less were DC lobbyists in 2012, only 12 per cent are younger than 35 (Rehr 2012).
findings.numbers: 30,000 lobbyists (2012); 12% under 35

findings.finding: Revolving door: about 52 per cent of these lobbyists came through government, and 48 per cent of those held two or more government positions (LaPira and Thomas 2014, as cited).
findings.numbers: 52% revolving door; 48% of those with 2+ government positions

findings.numbers: 37% knew next to nothing about LDA/HLOGA

findings.numbers: About 1.5 feet of paper per office per day

Furnas et al. find low overlap between organisational lobbying and PAC spending. That gives empirical weight to the paper's unquantified claim (citing Koger and Victor) that few lobbyists engage in campaign finance.

Kalla and Broockman's field experiment shows contributions buy access. It qualifies the paper's view that campaign finance matters little: money matters for access, not necessarily for votes, which is the flip model's stance.
Bacik et al. measure lobbyist networks over time, the empirical counterpart to the paper's argument that a lobbyist's value is their relationship portfolio.
Both draw on Hula (1999). The paper says informed lobbyists attract coalition partners, and Pritoni's review covers the determinants of coalitions, including information and brokers.
Both cover how interest-group signals reach overloaded congressional offices. The paper gives the messaging advice and Box-Steffensmeier measures cue-taking from Dear Colleague letters.

works.title: Lobbying coalitions and their determinants: a systematic literature review
works.summary:
Pritoni, Bitonti and Montalbano run a PRISMA-ScR scoping review of 80 English-language political science and public administration articles on lobbying coalitions, published 1985-2023 and indexed in Web of Science. Sixteen of those articles, contributing 77 hypotheses, enter a vote-count meta-analysis. Large-N quantitative designs dominate the field: 42 of 80 articles (52.5%). Social network analysis appears in only 4 of 80 (5%), and QCA in none. Most studies define coalitions by behavior: 59 of 80 use behavioral coordination, 12 use policy camp and 6 use formal organization. Across all 77 hypotheses, 57 are supported (74%). That figure pools US and EU studies and is UNSTRATIFIED by polity. By level, support is meso 11/14, micro 35/45 and macro 10/16. The 'weapon of the weak' hypothesis is supported in 11 of 12 tests, though a minority of studies find the reverse, and the authors suggest a minimum-resource threshold. Issue context is supported 6/7, ideology 6/7 and third-party brokers 3/3. The SNA-based tests have the weakest record of any design, 5 of 9 supported (55.6%). The review studies only why groups form coalitions. It calls the evidence on whether coalitions win contradictory and leaves that question to future work.

For Paul's systems, the paper matters because the coalitions it studies are coalitions among interest groups. Melange's 'coalitions' are mostly blocs of legislators: Ward clusters on press lean, signed partitions, and cosponsor spread. Read strictly, the review supports two narrower points about how Melange models the industries themselves. First, coalition alignment depends on the issue, which favors the per-bill contested registry over fixed global sides. Second, the CU side is modeled as a lone actor, even though the literature says weaker groups pool resources. The review gives no evidence that coalitions raise influence, so neither point justifies adding allied money as a weight.
works.question: RQ1: What are the key characteristics and trends of research in the academic debate on lobbying coalitions? RQ2: What are the main explanations used to account for interest groups' choice to form or join a coalition? (p. 3)
works.method: PRISMA-ScR scoping review protocol (Tricco et al. 2018) with descriptive counts (year, venue, polity, design, definitions) and a vote-count style meta-analysis: for each hypothesis, supported or not supported; confirmation rate = supported / total by level, factor and decade. Intercoder reliability by Krippendorff's alpha on 8 randomly selected articles (10% of sample): K-alpha = 0.889 (p. 4). Decade assignment uses article publication year.

Most-receptive venues are Interest Groups & Advocacy and the Journal of European Public Policy.

This is the earlier two-group signed-partition method on legislator cosponsorship backbones. It works at the legislator level, so Pritoni's group-level determinants do not transfer to it.

The component-literature map cites Romero Moreno 2021 for the contested-bills component (it models a controller against a fixed opponent). Pritoni supplies the empirical case for setting counterparties per issue rather than globally.

The component-literature map cites it alongside Pritoni for melange-sna.press-coalition-ward. It infers communities from shared text, which is a policy-camp-style definition, not coordination.

works.title: Measuring Interest Group Positions on Legislation: An AI-Driven Analysis of Lobbying Reports
works.summary:
Kim, Kim, Jeong, Oh and In Song Kim (arXiv 2025, PNAS-format draft) label which way interest groups lean on individual bills, using the free-text bill lines in LDA quarterly reports from 2009 to 2022 (111th-117th Congresses). The pipeline has two stages. GPT-4 at temperature 0 labels keyword-filtered lines, producing 82,421 positions. A heterogeneous GraphSAGE model then fills in where the text is unclear, producing 196,683 more, about 70.5% of the total. The final dataset has 279,104 group-by-bill positions covering 12,032 groups and 42,475 bills, labelled Support, Oppose, or Engage (Engage merges Amend and Monitor). The LLM agrees with human coders 96.9% of the time, but only on the 391 items where both coders agreed. It matches MapLight on 91% of 1,182 overlapping pairs. The GNN reaches 78.5% accuracy, and Oppose is its weakest class (F1 64). On the substance:
- Support rises toward enactment.
- Oppose and Amend rise late in bills that go on to fail. That finding rests on 3 vetoed bills.
- Comparing firms at the 90th and 10th percentiles of size, larger firms are 19.5 pp more likely to lobby and 4.5 pp more likely to Monitor.
- A one-dimensional IRT score for groups (LPscore) correlates only weakly with DIME CFscores (r = 0.19, n = 218).

This matters here because the system has already taken in this dataset and copied its method. It downloaded the Dataverse release, rebuilt Kim's labelling step with Haiku, and benchmarked it against Kim's published labels at natural base rates. On that benchmark, Support and Oppose come out weak (precision 0.42, recall 0.49) and Amend is never recovered. That result led to the standing rule that inferred positions are evidence for retrieval and adjudication, never automatic weights. The paper's real value to Paul is as calibration gold for 2009-2022 and as raw material for per-bill industry conflict, which the system already computes. It is not a feed that can be wired straight into the graph.
works.question: Can the positions that U.S. interest groups take on individual bills (Support, Oppose, or Engage, where Engage = Amend + Monitor) be measured directly from Lobbying Disclosure Act reports across all bills from the 111th to 117th Congresses? The paper then asks how those positions vary by legislative stage, firm size, bill subject, and industry.
works.method: (1) LLM labelling: GPT-4 via Azure OpenAI at temperature 0, zero-shot prompt with bill ID, short and official titles, and lobbying text. Five labels in the LLM stage (Support, Oppose, Amend, Monitor, Mention); Mention covers ambiguous or non-amending activity. (2) GNN refinement: heterogeneous GraphSAGE (SI Table 9: 3 classes, hidden size 90, ELU, dropout 0.2, concat decoder) predicts the interest group-bill link type (Support, Oppose, Engage). Amend and Monitor are merged into Engage because four-class accuracy on Amend was low. Training uses LLM labels plus MapLight labels, with a 7:1:2 split. Seventeen graph configurations are compared (base graph; add sponsors, legislators, registrants, lobbyists, related bills, and combinations); the best is base graph + legislator-lobbyist. Predictions are kept as proxy labels only when class probability exceeds 0.9. (3) LPscores: graded-response IRT (Samejima; R mirt) on Support and Oppose labels, with Engage excluded, after keeping groups with at least 10 bills and bills with at least 10 groups. (4) Analyses: descriptive position shares by legislative stage (Fig 2; stage timing proxied by quarterly report deadline); logistic regression for the decision to lobby and Dirichlet regression for position composition, with predicted-probability differences between firms at the 90th and 10th employment percentiles (Fig 3; year FE; optional NAICS FE, PPENT, COGS; SI Tables 19-20); descriptive position ratios by subject (Fig 4, SI Table 21); LPscore distributions by industry (Fig 5); bill-level latent-score scatter and KDE (Fig 6); Pearson correlation with DIME CFscores (n=218).

Same LobbyView group (In Song Kim is a co-author). It studies how the lobbying network evolves over time, while this paper measures each group's position on each bill.

works.title: Conflating Lobbying and PACs: The Surprisingly Low Overlap in Organizational Lobbying and Campaign Expenditures
works.summary:
Furnas, LaPira and Brock (PS, Oct 2025) put Center for Responsive Politics LDA lobbying records and FEC records of organization and affiliated-PAC giving side by side for each organization, 1998-2018. Most politically active organizations do only one of the two. In 1998 (n=9,076 organizations), 64% only lobbied, 24% only gave through a PAC and 12% did both. By 2008 (n=15,729) the split was 70/20/10. Pooled over 1998-2018, 3,427 of 54,517 organizations (6.3%) did both. That denominator is the extractor's sum of the Figure 4 counts.

Within that minority sits most of the lobbying money. About 75% of lobbying spending in 1998-2018 came from organizations that also gave through a PAC. Their mean yearly lobbying spend was $403k, against $64k for organizations that only lobbied. Going the other way, the share of PAC dollars that came from lobbying organizations fell from over 65% in 1998 to about 30% in 2018. Employee giving, Super PACs and dark money are excluded. The paper is purely descriptive: no model, no identification strategy, and nothing about access or votes.

For Paul's systems the paper matters in three ways:

- **FEC as a stand-in for lobbying.** Across the population, campaign money is a poor proxy for lobbying. That supports the twice-locked rule that FEC exposure is never presented as a lobbying predictor. It also argues against reading the 42-month figure as a lead time: in the code it is only how much fresher the FEC data is than the LDA data.
- **The flip model's competitor-money leg.** That leg counts only PAC money. It can see the large trade associations, which almost all have PACs. It cannot see organizations that lobby without a PAC.
- **Mentat's counts.** Mentat matches individual employee giving by employer string. The paper's definition of organizational giving excludes employees, so its overlap figures do not carry over to Mentat's totals without first aligning the two definitions.
works.question: Are campaign contributions (PAC giving) and lobbying complements, substitutes, or unrelated forms of organizational political engagement? Empirically: how much do the interest groups that lobby overlap with the groups that contribute through PACs, and which types of organizations do each?
works.method: Descriptive only. Figure 1: yearly share of organizations that are lobby-only, PAC-only, or both. Figure 2: share of yearly lobbying expenditures and of PAC contributions by group type. Figure 3: distributions of average yearly PAC contributions (3a) and average yearly lobbying spending (3b) by group type, shown as dot plots with violin density, mean, IQR and 2.5/97.5 percentiles. Figure 4: log-log scatter of total lobbying spending against total PAC contributions per organization, with marginal histograms, coloured by the four activity categories. No regression, hypothesis test, or model is reported.

findings.finding: Most politically active organizations engage in only one of the two activities; only a small minority do both. The abstract states the headline finding, and the results section gives the counts.
findings.numbers: 1998 (n=9,076 orgs): 24% PAC-only, 64% lobby-only, 12% both. Around 2008 (n=15,729 orgs): 20% PAC-only, 70% lobby-only, 10% both. Percentages in each year sum to 100, so the categories are treated as exclusive.

findings.finding: Pooled over 1998-2018, only a small share of organizations do both.
findings.numbers: Lobby-only ~34,000 (n=34,038); PAC-only ~9,500 (n=9,528); registered but not active ~7,500 (n=7,524); both n=3,427 = 6.3% of the 54,517 total (6.3% is stated in the text; the 54,517 denominator is the extractor's sum).

findings.finding: Lobbying money is concentrated among organizations that also make PAC contributions, but that share fell over time.
findings.numbers: About 75% of lobbying expenditures (1998-2018) came from organizations that also contributed through PACs. The share of PAC contributions coming from organizations that also lobby fell from more than 65% in 1998 to about 30% in 2018.
