works.title: Moneyed Interests, Information, and Action in Congress: A Survey Experiment
works.summary:
Furnas, LaPira, Hertel-Fernandez, Drutman and Kosar ran a 4 x 2 x 4 factorial vignette inside the 2017 Congressional Capacity Survey. The sample is 441 DC staffers, a 5.2% response rate (441 of 8,485), with 549 ratings per factor. Each vignette varied who made the request (constituent, campaign donor, consumer-group lobbyist or business lobbyist), what they asked for (propose a bill or stop one) and what evidence they brought (supportive polling, their own analysis, or a center-left or center-right think tank). Effects are AMCEs estimated by weighted OLS with HC3 errors. Figures 2-5 are plots, so the text gives no coefficient values.

Findings. Requester identity barely changes whether staff will take a meeting, and donors get no more meetings than constituents, which runs against Kalla and Broockman. Staff say they are less likely to use information from donors. Pooled across all staff, think-tank evidence does little for whether staff side with the requester. Split by party, the effect appears: staff side with evidence from their own side's think tank, and evidence from the other side costs about twice what aligned evidence gains. Staff in both parties side more often with requests to stop a bill than to propose one. Everything is stated intention about a hypothetical request, and the design is underpowered. After FDR correction, 46 of 11,904 pairwise tests survive.

For Paul's systems, the paper bears mainly on the partisan source-alignment factor (cpf_pressure 1.7/0.5, whose code comment cites "Furnas/Bakker") and on the flip model's premise that money buys access. It does not calibrate either one. The paper's manipulation is the ideology of an outside requester's evidence as judged by staff, not a co-partisan legislator applying pressure. Its asymmetry also runs the other way from the system's. Two places in the system attribute claims to this paper that it does not make: "money is capped, info is the lever" and "district-relevant information".
works.question: Whether and how congressional staffers respond to a lobbying-style request depending on (a) the identity of the requester (constituent, donor to the Member's campaign, national consumer-group lobbyist, large national business lobbyist), (b) the action requested (propose a new bill, or stop a bill under consideration), and (c) the supporting information offered (supportive constituency polling, the requester's own analysis, or jobs evidence from a center-left or center-right think tank). Four outcomes: likelihood of taking a meeting, of using the information for the boss's recommendations, of siding with the requester in the recommendation, and of rating the requester as representative of the district or state.
works.method: Fully randomised 4 x 2 x 4 factorial vignette (32 possible conditions) with four dependent variables, each a five-point Likert item transformed to numeric. Following Hainmueller, Hopkins and Yamamoto (2014), the authors estimate the Average Marginal Component Effect (AMCE) of each factor level by OLS, using post-stratification weights and HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (p.9). Subgroup models for all staff, Democratic staff and Republican staff. The preregistered design called for 32-condition pairwise t-tests; the sample was underpowered for that, so these are reported in Appendix B. Appendix B: 11,904 pairwise tests (992 pairs x 4 outcomes, plus partisan subsamples); 828 pairs nominally significant at alpha 0.10; 46 pairs survive Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction at 0.10 (Table 1). Significant pairwise differences appear only for the "recommend the boss side with petitioner" and "representative" outcomes, mostly in the partisan subsamples and mostly between opposite-valence information sources. Figures 2 to 5 plot AMCEs with baseline categories: constituent, supportive polling, propose bill. Weights: post-stratification on chamber, office type and party from the LegiStorm frame; a second weight (psweight_g) conditions on gender because of persistent gender imbalance (Appendix A).

findings.finding: Taking a meeting (lowest-stakes outcome): most identity effects are not statistically distinguishable from zero. Democratic staff are less likely to take meetings with donors. Staff are less likely than constituents to take meetings with donors or lobbyists overall, but the authors read this as evidence that donors are not granted meetings more readily than constituents, and they flag social desirability. No relationship with information source or requested action.
findings.numbers: Figure 2 gives AMCEs only as a plot; no point estimates in the extracted text. Dependent variable: five-point Likert, numerically transformed.

findings.finding: Using the information provided: staff report being much less likely to use information from donors, especially Democratic staff. The only statistically distinguishable Democratic-Republican gap is for evidence from a center-right think tank. Other identity, action and information effects are not distinguishable from zero.
findings.numbers: No point estimates in the text; Democratic-Republican difference reported only qualitatively.

findings.finding: Siding with the requester in the recommendation to the boss (highest commitment): across all staff there is minimal evidence that think-tank information raises the chance of siding with the requester, and staff may be less likely to side with partisan-aligned groups than with individuals offering their own analysis. Disaggregated by party, Democrats are substantially more likely to side with center-left think tanks and less likely with center-right ones; Republicans show the mirror pattern. Offering information from a non-aligned think tank yields roughly twice the penalty of the benefit from an aligned one.
findings.numbers: 'Roughly twice' is the only ratio given; no coefficient values in the text.

findings.finding: Requests to stop a bill: both Democratic and Republican staff are more likely to side with requesters who want to stop a bill than with those proposing one. The authors offer several explanations (visibility of proposing bills, skepticism about legislation, status-quo bias from veto points, selectivity given many requests) and do not separate them.
findings.location: Results p.14 and Discussion p.18; Figure 4
findings.numbers: Not given in the text.

findings.finding: Perceived representativeness: all staff rate donors, business lobbyists and consumer lobbyists as less representative of their district or state than constituents. Exceptions: no distinguishable effect among Republican staff for donors or business lobbyists, and among Democratic staff for consumer lobbyists. Both parties rate presenters of aligned think-tank evidence as more representative than presenters of constituency polling supporting the staffer's own position. Republicans rate center-left presenters as less representative; Democrats' ratings of center-right presenters do not differ from polling presenters.
findings.numbers: Figure 5 AMCEs are plotted only; no point estimates in the text.

findings.finding: Staff are more likely to side with donors than to meet with or use information from donors, relative to constituents. The authors say this 'merits further inquiry' and do not resolve whether donors qua donors have direct influence.
findings.numbers: Not given in the text.

related.why: Kalla & Broockman's field experiment finds revealed donors get more senior-staff access. This paper's survey experiment finds donors get no meeting advantage over constituents (p.9) and sets itself explicitly against Kalla and Broockman; it cites them (p.17) for the chief of staff being the most likely to grant donor meetings.

The system pairs the two papers as 'Furnas/Bakker source-alignment' for cpf_pressure and the lt-priming cross-party cue gate. Bakker covers partisan cue receptivity; Furnas covers staff reception of evidence from aligned and non-aligned sources.
Same author. It shows low overlap between lobbying and PAC spending, which is consistent with this paper's separation of donor identity from information-based lobbying.
Both study interest-group signals as cues inside Congress: Dear Colleague endorsements there, think-tank evidence here.

Holyoke et al. treat lobbying as largely relationship building. This paper adds staff-side evidence that the information a lobbyist brings, and its ideological source, shapes siding; its point that lobbyists are more persistent than donors is the authors' speculation (p.17), not a finding.

works.title: Mapping Political Communities: A Statistical Analysis of Lobbying Networks in Legislative Politics
works.summary:
Kim and Kunisky propose the Bipartite Link Community Model (biLCM). It is a Poisson model of a two-mode count matrix in which each interaction between an interest group and a politician is assigned to one of k latent "link communities". This allows mixed memberships, where an actor belongs to several communities, and mixed interactions, where one pair interacts in several communities. The model is fitted by EM with 50 random starts and k = 8. The application covers the 113th Congress only. A_ij counts the bills that group i lobbied and politician j sponsored, so the network is built indirectly because LD-2 reports never name the members contacted. The paper finds eight legislation communities that match committee jurisdictions. Specialists (MICROSOFT and ARCH COAL, at least 85% in one community) coexist with generalists (the CHAMBER OF COMMERCE, no community above 25%). Generalists and senior leaders cluster on power committees. Civil Society is the only cross-industry domain. The paper concludes that narrow industry interest drives most lobbying. A latent space model and a dc-biSBM recover the same blocks but miss mixed membership.

For Paul's systems, the most direct point is this. The paper's lobbying network uses the same construction as Melange's lobbied-member link: an organisation is credited to a member through a bill roster. The paper never treats that link as contact or influence, which backs the system's ruling that the link is circular. Three other bearings qualify claims the system makes. First, the dashboard cites the paper for "exploitable community structure" in the cosponsor graph, but the paper's communities are group-by-member lobbying communities, and budgetRecruit has no community term. Second, co-lobbying cannot separate lobbying for a bill from lobbying against it, so the paper cannot identify rival-industry champions. Third, leaders' broad memberships show how widely they draw lobbying, not leverage on credit-union issues. Everything here is descriptive, comes from one Congress, and is not causal.
works.question: How can latent memberships of political actors in the communities that drive their observable interactions be inferred, when the network is bipartite, actors hold several memberships, and a pair of actors can interact in several ways? Application: which legislation communities organize interest-group lobbying of legislators in the 113th Congress, and when do domain-specific groups lobby outside their domain?
works.method: Bipartite Link Community Model (biLCM): A_ij ~ Poisson(sum over z of kappa_z * alpha_iz * beta_jz), with z = 1..k link communities (eq. 1, p. 5). Estimation by EM with ancillary parameters q_ij(z) (eqs. 2-5, p. 6). Normalisation: sum_i alpha_iz = sum_j beta_jz = 1 for each z. k = 8 communities, chosen with reference to community structure seen in the latent space model (fn. 11). 50 random starts; highest likelihood kept (p. 6). Membership shares p_iz and q_jz are normalised kappa_z-weighted alphas and betas; entropy H in bits, with about 2^H communities actively used (p. 9). Comparison models: (a) 2-D latent space model with Poisson mean exp(alpha_i + beta_j - ||theta_i - psi_j||^2), Bayesian in Stan with hierarchical priors (eq. 6, pp. 12-13); (b) degree-corrected bipartite SBM (dc-biSBM), EM from Larremore et al. (2014), k = l = 8, 50 starts (eq. 7, pp. 15-16). Significance: permutation test against a null that keeps actor-level activity distributions (p. 12). Anomalies: observed versus biLCM-estimated counts, ranked by deviation (Table 1, p. 11).

findings.finding: Eight legislation communities are named by their leading groups: Healthcare, Veterans' Affairs, Technology & Telecommunications, Energy, Finance & Insurance, Universities & Research, Civil Society, and Retail & Transportation.
findings.location: p. 7, paragraph 'We name the legislation communities'

findings.finding: Specialist groups lobby a single community; generalists spread across several. MICROSOFT and ARCH COAL interact with one community at probability of at least 85%. MCAFEE interacts with Technology & Telecom at 31% and Universities & Research at 52%. PHILIPS NORTH AMERICA and the CHAMBER OF COMMERCE have no single community above 25%.
findings.numbers: MICROSOFT, ARCH COAL: at least 85% in one community; MCAFEE: 31% and 52%; PHILIPS and CHAMBER: at most 25% per community

findings.finding: Specialist and generalist interest groups coexist. Targeted groups lobby committees with narrow jurisdiction; broad groups target power committees (Ways and Means, Senate Appropriations).
findings.numbers: not stated as a single statistic

findings.finding: Only one broad issue area is lobbied by diverse groups: Civil Society, covering social and human-rights legislation. It is the fourth most active of eight communities by kappa_z, so it accounts for only a modest share of lobbying activity.
findings.numbers: fourth of 8 by kappa_z

findings.finding: Politicians with high entropy, meaning membership in at least four communities, sit on power committees such as Ways and Means and Senate Appropriations, which control the power of the purse.
findings.numbers: entropy at least 2 corresponds to at least 4 communities; 52% of the 113th Congress were Republican (Figure 4 caption)

findings.finding: Politicians interacting with a community at probability at least 40% sit on committees matching its subject (e.g. Financial Services for Finance & Insurance; Armed Services for the defence-related group).
findings.numbers: threshold of 40% for committee groups

related.why: The paper's lobbying dataset is distilled from LobbyView (cited as Kim 2018) and shares its NLP bill-identification pipeline.
Supplies signed bill positions from LDA text, which Kim-Kunisky say their data lack (no for/against distinction).
Kim-Kunisky cite Porter et al. 2005 when proposing biLCM for networks of legislators and committees; both are also cited together in the brain-vault dashboard capstone note (not in dashboard code).
Also built from LobbyView (co-authored by In Song Kim), as a yearly multi-layer network over time, where Kim-Kunisky give a single-Congress (113th) snapshot.
A hypergraph treatment of a lobby network; Kim-Kunisky list multi-partite (group-politician-bill) extension as future work.
Signed partitioning of the House co-sponsorship network supplies a sign Kim-Kunisky's co-lobbying lacks, but is a hard partition without mixed membership.

works.title: The Effects of Firms' Lobbying on Resource Misallocation
works.summary:
Huneeus and Kim link federal LDA lobbying reports (1999-2015 filings, about 972k report rows) to US public firms in Compustat. They ask two questions: does lobbying make a firm bigger, and what does that cost the economy in productivity?

**Descriptive facts**
- Lobbying is rare: 766 of 7,646 public firms lobbied in 2017.
- It is very persistent: more than 80% of 2016 lobbyists lobbied again in 2017, with an intensive-margin slope of 0.922.
- It runs to more than 6 times PAC-type campaign contributions.
- Most bills draw a median of 2 lobbying clients.

**Causal estimate.** The instrument is a shift-share. For each firm it combines its lagged share of lobbied bills going to each committee with the committee seats held by politicians from its headquarters state. The IV elasticity of sales on lobbying is 0.319 for all years (first-stage F 14.3) and 0.227 after 2007 (F 13.1). OLS gives about 0.04-0.05. The paper's "3 percent per 10 percent" headline uses the full-sample estimate, while its stated preferred estimate is 0.2 percent per 1 percent.

**Structural model.** A Hsieh-Klenow/Melitz model is fitted by SMM with an identity weighting matrix. With sigma_C fixed at 4, removing the return to lobbying raises aggregate productivity by 22%. That figure moves from 38% to 13% as sigma_C goes from 2 to 6.

**What it means for Paul's systems.** Nothing here estimates how a member of Congress responds to money. The usable pieces are narrower:
- The committee-relevance weight is computed from data, where the committee pillar's tier weights are owner judgment.
- The persistence facts explain why naive carry-forward is hard to beat in Mentat's lobbying forecasts.
- The paper's causal direction (lobbying leads to revenue) is a simultaneity warning for the sector-growth study's growth-leads-to-lobbying regressions.
- Appendix A's fuzzy matching with a 5% random validation sample is a template for auditing the LDA client classifier.

All transfers are UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until a second path reproduces them.
works.question: Does firms' lobbying causally increase firm size, and how much does lobbying reduce aggregate productivity through misallocation of resources across firms (distortion of firm size)? (Abstract; Introduction, printed pp.1-3)
works.method: Descriptive stylized facts (Section 2); OLS and IV panel regressions of log sales and log profits on log lobbying expenditure with firm, year and state-year fixed effects, standard errors double-clustered by firm and year (Table 2, Appendix F); structural model estimated by simulated method of moments (nine parameters: production and lobbying fixed costs, variances and covariances of productivity and wedge, and beta), with sigma_C=4, death rate 0.025 and beta_s=beta imposed (pp.27-31); counterfactual with beta=0 and a sensitivity sweep over sigma_C (pp.31-32). The SMM text says the weighting matrix is the generalized inverse of the moment covariance, but for now it uses the identity matrix (fn.22, p.29).

findings.finding: Lobbying is rare: only 766 of 7,646 public US firms lobbied in 2017; average share of public firms lobbying across years is 11.8 percent (text figure; 766/7,646 is about 10.0 percent for 2017 alone).
findings.numbers: 766 of 7,646 firms (2017); 11.8 percent average; manufacturing 15.8 percent lobby, 6.5 percent in-house

findings.finding: Lobbying spending exceeds campaign contributions: on average lobbying is more than six times larger than campaign contributions (PAC, party, candidate and other federal committee contributions; individual contributions excluded).
findings.numbers: more than 6x on average (2 year cycles, 1999-2016)

findings.finding: Firm size and lobbying are positively correlated on the intensive margin (conditional on lobbying).
findings.numbers: log lobbying coefficient on log sales = 0.984 (p=0.000, t=28.13)

findings.finding: Lobbying is highly persistent. More than 80 percent of firms that lobbied in 2016 lobbied in 2017; the intensive-margin correlation of log lobbying across adjacent years is high, though persistence dropped during 2007-2009.
findings.numbers: >80 percent (2016 to 2017); intensive margin coefficient 0.922 (t=157.88)

findings.finding: Firm-level lobbying exceeds lobbying by business and industry organizations (figure only; no dollar totals stated in the text).
findings.numbers: none stated in text

findings.finding: Most congressional bills are lobbied by only one or two interest groups (narrow, firm-specific lobbying).
findings.location: Fact 6, Figure 5, Table C.1, printed pp.11-12
findings.numbers: median 2 clients per bill; mean 3.45 clients across 65,047 bills; trade bills: 1,862 bills, mean 3.21, median 2

related.why: LobbyView is the firm-name-disambiguated LDA and bill database that this paper builds on and releases (confirmed from the item title). Ingestion by collect_lobbyview.py was not checked.
Same LobbyView firm linkage, joined to FEC donations, bearing on the lobbying-to-contribution relation in H&K Fact 2. Checked only by title and authors.
Survey of empirical lobbying models, including returns-to-lobbying designs and the Grossman-Helpman microfoundation that H&K Section 3.2 generalizes.
Links corporate lobbying and PACs to market concentration, a related misallocation question at industry level. The outcome differs from H&K's firm-size distortion.
Its two-way fixed-effects caution applies to H&K's OLS columns (firm, year and state-year FE) and to the system's sector-growth regressions.
Finds low overlap between organizational lobbying and PAC spending, which qualifies any use of H&K's lobbying-to-contribution ratio.
Models committee assignment as a matching process, bearing on H&K's identifying assumption that committee moves are exogenous to firms.
Network analysis of House committees, relevant to H&K's committee-share weights. Checked only by title and authors.

works.title: Mathematical Modeling, Analysis and Simulation Utilizing Machine Learning Tools for Assessing the Impact of Climate Lobbying
works.summary:
Jacoby et al. (arXiv 2505.09617, 2025) model a legislature the way an epidemic model tracks a population. Each legislator sits in one of four compartments: not yet introduced (S), undecided centrist (C), yes (Y) or no (N). Undecided members move to Y or N through mass-action contact with members who have already decided. The extended model adds lobbyist counts and lobbying money (L_F, L_A, M_F, M_A) and drains campaign donations (I_F, I_A). Every parameter is fixed from earlier literature (Table 2); none is estimated. The model is checked against one bill, the 2009 Waxman-Markey vote (ACESA).

In the House, the baseline run gives 230 yes, 196 no and 9 undecided, against an actual 219 to 212. Adding donations moves 1 member. Adding lobbying resolves 8 more undecided members (231 yes, 203 no, 1 undecided). The Senate barely changes. The analysis shows that the centrist-flow and centrist-lobbying parameters (M_LF, M_LA) drive the outcome. An SVM finds no clean pass/fail boundary. Widening the centrist ideology band from ±0.25 to ±0.35 reverses the House result.

For Paul's system this is weak evidence. Each chamber has one comparison point, every "effect" is the output of parameters the authors chose, and the paper's claim of accuracy within 5% does not hold against its own errors of 5.02%, 5.48% and 7.55%. Its useful content is structural, not empirical:
- Legislators who have already decided are treated as fixed, and only undecided members move. This matches the low PERS values for Champion and Opponent.
- Who counts as movable decides the result. The system already found the same thing when it swept PERS_NONE.
- The sensitivity harness does not sweep the flip model's WM/WP channel weights or the PERS table. The paper says centrist-flow parameters are the ones that matter, so those are the obvious next sweeps.

The lobbying-versus-donations contrast should not be imported into the flip model. It is a contrast between simulation runs, not an estimate. Its lobbyist counts also come from revolving-door staff, and project rules bar LDA as an edge or weight source (D-021).
works.question: Can a compartmental differential-equation model of legislators (not yet introduced, undecided centrists, yes, no), extended with lobbyists, lobbying money, and campaign donations, simulate and predict roll-call passage, and how do lobbying and donations change outcomes? Stated objectives (a) build the model, (b) study how interactions shape legislative behavior, (c) predict likelihood of passage (p.3).
works.method: Deterministic ODE system. Baseline model (eqs 2.1a-d, p.4-5) and extended model with lobbyists L_F, L_A, money M_F, M_A and donations I_F, I_A (eqs 2.2a-h, p.6-7). Well-posedness: positivity via an invariant-domain lemma stated in the text (p.7-8) and boundedness via M(t) = S + C + Y + N constant (p.8). Stability: linearization about (0, C0, 0, 0) (unstable) and (0, 0, Y0, N0) (stable), in Sec 3.1 (p.10) and Sec 3.2.2 (p.12), with closed-form L_F(t), L_A(t) (Sec 3.2.1, p.11). Simulation: no solver, software or numerical tolerance stated. Sensitivity: 10% variation of centrist-flow parameters with distributions of final C, Y, N (Sec 4, p.12-13); parameter sweeps labelled pass/fail and separated by linear SVM (Sec 4.1-4.2, p.14-17); individual parameter impact ranking (Sec 4.3, Fig 12, p.18-19). Ideology sensitivity via centrist band (Sec 5.3, p.20-21). Validation: compare simulated final House and Senate counts to actual tallies using percent error (Sec 5.1, p.19-20).

findings.finding: Baseline House simulation with no lobbying or donations: model settles at yes/no/undecided counts, compared with actual tally.
findings.numbers: Model 230 yes, 196 no, 9 undecided vs actual 219 yes, 212 no, 4 abstain; percent error 5.02% (yes), 7.55% (no).

findings.finding: Adding campaign donations alone changes almost nothing; authors conclude donations have limited impact on passage.
findings.numbers: 231 yes, 196 no, 8 undecided (one undecided legislator moves to yes).

findings.finding: Adding lobbying (with donations) moves the House prediction closer to the actual count; authors attribute the shift mainly to lobbying converting undecided legislators.
findings.numbers: 231 yes, 203 no, 1 undecided; percent error 5.48% (yes), 4.25% (no). Undecided fell from 9 to 1, i.e., 8 legislators resolved in total.

findings.finding: Senate baseline and extended runs barely differ; authors say lobbying has minimal effect in the Senate, which they read as consistent with ACESA failing against the 60-vote filibuster threshold.
findings.numbers: Baseline 52 yes, 47 no, 1 undecided; with lobbying and donations 52 yes, 48 no, 0 undecided. No Senate actual tally is given in the text.

findings.finding: Stability: the all-undecided point is unstable; the point with Y and N positive and S, C at zero is stable, so Y and N converge to positive constants and the legislature tends toward a decision. Same qualitative result holds with lobbying and donations included.
findings.numbers: No numeric equilibrium values for Y0 or N0 are reported in the text.

findings.finding: Sensitivity to a 10% change in centrist flow parameters: final C, Y, N look roughly normally distributed; trajectories cross the actual House vote count, which authors read as robustness.
findings.numbers: Parameters varied by 10%; no summary statistics beyond the figures are given in the text.

related.why: Jacoby cites Bonica's roll-call inference paper [5], not the 2013 paper, for the claim that donations may reflect ideology rather than influence (p.20). The 2013 paper is Paul's on-disk anchor for that ideological-money reading but is not itself cited, so the relation is complements, not cites.

Kalla and Broockman provide experimental evidence that money buys access. Jacoby's finding that donations barely move votes is a simulated parallel with no causal design, and Kalla is the stronger basis for the flip model's WM < WP. Not cited by Jacoby.

Jacoby cites Poole and Rosenthal [19] for spatial models and Voteview [16] for the alpha rates (Table 2). This vault item (D-NOMINATE after 10 years) is not itself cited; the centrist-band reversal plausibly depends on that kind of ideal-point scale, though the paper does not name the scale it used.
Jacoby's sensitivity runs are deterministic sweeps of 1000 samples. Monte Carlo practice is the stochastic extension the authors say would enhance the model (p.22). Not cited by Jacoby.

Furnas et al. separate lobbying from PAC spending at the organization level. Jacoby's lobbying-versus-donations split rests on parameter choices, not on data that separates the two channels. Not cited by Jacoby.

works.title: Systemic and Sequential Links between Campaign Donations and Lobbying
works.summary:
Kim, Stuckatz and Wolters build a firm-politician-year panel. It covers 2,703 publicly traded manufacturing firms and 979 members of Congress from 2008 to 2018. Lobbying comes from parsed LDA reports that name bills, and donations come from FEC records. The question is whether a firm's first donation to a member in a 3-year window is followed by the firm lobbying bills that the member sponsors, co-sponsors, or that go to the member's committees.

**Fixed-effects results.** The models compare firm-politician pairs within the same politician. A new donation goes with a 2.3 to 4.8 percentage-point higher chance of that lobbying. The base rate is about 0.07. These are pooled estimates (UNSTRATIFIED by chamber or donor type).

**Matched difference-in-differences.** These results are split by chamber. Senate estimates rise from 7.5 pp at t+0 to 11 pp at t+3. House estimates rise from 8.6 to 12.7 pp.

**Donor type and channel.** The link is strongest for corporate PAC money and for lobbying tied to committees. For PACs, committee-linked lobbying rises from 0.103 to 0.147. CEO and employee donations show much weaker links, and lobbying does not predict later donations. Only about 5% of public firms both donate and lobby (2013).

**Limits.** The authors say plainly that the results are associations, not causal effects. The lobbying measure reaches the member only through who sponsors the bill or which committee gets it, because LDA filings never name members.

**What it means for Melange.**
- It is the closest published counterpart to the closed FEC x LDA bridge test. The paper uses a different unit (firm-member pairs over time, not a member-level cross-section) and different fixed effects.
- It also points to a gap. The paper's strongest channel, committee referral, is missing from the system's LobbyView outcome, which counts only sponsor and cosponsor links. And the system's own committee control may absorb that channel.
- It supports the engine's choice to measure money from direct PACs only, and the "money buys access" stance as a weak prior. It does not speak to votes or flips.

All of this is UNVERIFIED agent analysis until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
works.question: Do special-interest groups (mainly publicly traded firms, their corporate PACs and their employees) donate to members of Congress whom they later lobby on related bills? The paper tests a sequential "access-buying" link: a first-time donation to a politician is followed by lobbying on bills sponsored by, co-sponsored by, or assigned to committees of that same politician.
works.method: (1) Linear probability model with fixed effects (Eq. 2, Table 1, App.H). Outcome: firm lobbies a bill tied to politician j in year t through sponsorship, co-sponsorship or committee. works.title: Corporate lobbying, political action committees, and market concentration
works.summary: Bickmore, Blau, Griffith and Whitby (Public Choice, 2025) ask whether corporate lobbying and PAC giving raise a firm's share of its NAICS industry. They merge Compustat with Center for Responsive Politics lobbying and PAC data for 1998-2016 (237,849 firm-years; 116,242 with full controls). Lobbying appears in 4.23 percent of firm-years. With industry and year fixed effects, firm-clustered errors and no firm fixed effects, a lobbying firm's share of industry assets is 0.0743 higher (Table 3, full controls; 0.0907 without controls). Because the outcome is a 0-1 share with mean 0.0727 and median 0.0010, that is 7.4 percentage points, about the size of the mean share. It is not a 7.4 percent relative rise. Results for market-cap and sales shares are similar. PAC contributors show about 0.11 higher share (election years, N = 62,198). Democratic and Republican giving show similar coefficients. Money to winning candidates is significant (0.062, SE 0.027) and money to losing candidates is not (0.040, SE 0.036), but the paper never tests the difference between the two. For causal evidence the authors use a difference-in-differences around the January 2006 Abramoff plea, 2003Q1-2009Q1. Lobbying firms' share falls 2.65 points (assets) and 3.36 points (market cap) relative to non-lobbyists. However, the pre-trend begins to bend in late 2004, and the placebo results appear only in figures. For Paul's systems this is firm-level evidence about economic returns to political activity. It does not measure member behaviour, and nothing in Melange measures market concentration. Its main use is as a caution on how the ROI and deep-pockets readings in Mentat's sector growth study and Melange's break-even widget are worded. The pooled estimate is UNSTRATIFIED by industry (interaction checks are described but not tabulated).

works.title: Lobbying ROI: An Analysis under the American Jobs Creation Act of 2004 (also: Measuring Rates of Return for Lobbying Expenditures)
works.summary:
Alexander, Scholz and Mazza study the one-time dividend repatriation deduction in the 2004 American Jobs Creation Act (s.965). They treat lobbying as an investment and divide estimated tax savings (amount repatriated x 35% x 85%) by each firm's LDA-reported lobbying spend. They used a "repat!" keyword search of 10-Ks for 2004-2006 to identify 476 repatriating firms, with dollar amounts for 450 (total $298bn). 93 of those firms lobbied. The headline ROI is about 220:1 ($62bn of savings on $282.7M of lobbying). Coalition members return 257:1 and solo lobbyists 154:1. Outliers drive the result: the per-company mean is 869:1 and the median 172:1. The lobbying denominator is an upper bound, and the design is purely cross-sectional, with no causal identification. Logit and OLS models (N=434 for the amount) show that size, profitability and operating cash flow predict who repatriated and how much. The abstract and conclusion say cash holdings do not matter, but Table 5 contradicts this (cash/assets 3.70, p<.001).

For Paul's systems this is a firm-side, policy-rent return on lobbying expenditure. It tells us nothing about how legislators respond, and it does not cover PAC contributions. Melange's "ROI" and break-even figures measure expected member flips per PAC dollar, so the 220:1 figure does not transfer to them. The paper does sharpen two points. First, its biggest returns came on an essentially uncontested provision, which bears on the contested-bills design. Second, its upper-bound denominator would double-count in-house and outside-firm LDA dollars that Mentat keeps separate. The paper is UNVERIFIED as a source for any Melange constant.
works.question: Do firms that lobbied for the AJCA s.965 one-time dividend repatriation deduction earn a measurable return on lobbying, and which firm characteristics predict whether and how much a firm repatriated?

(4) OLS of ln(amount repatriated) on the same regressors, N = 434, adjusted R2 = .48 (Table 5, fn 91). (5) Return on lobbying = estimated tax savings / estimated lobbying expense, with savings = amount repatriated x 35% x 85% (Table 6, Sec. III.B.2). Also a subsample of 48 firms spending over $1M.

works.title: Cue-Taking in Congress: Interest Group Signals from Dear Colleague Letters
works.summary: Box-Steffensmeier, Christenson and Craig (AJPS 63(1), 2019; online 2018) study 6,633 House bills that were the subject of supportive Dear Colleague letters, 106th to 111th Congresses (1999-2010; regression N = 6,597). They code the interest groups named as endorsers in each letter and measure two signals: Interest Group Social Power, the highest standardized eigenvector centrality of any endorser in the amicus curiae co-signing network, and Interest Group Count, the number of endorsers. In a negative binomial model of cosponsor counts with Congress fixed effects, both are positive (0.055 and 0.007, p<.001). Predicted cosponsors rise from 33 with no endorsement to 51 with a top-centrality endorser; 61 average-centrality endorsers are needed to match that. Logit models of committee reporting and House passage show no direct social-power effect. Count predicts passage (0.013) but not reporting. Cosponsor count predicts both later stages (0.002, 0.004). Majority-party sponsorship (1.353) and hot-bill status (2.428) are the largest passage predictors. The paper has no causal design. Endorsements may be solicited by the sponsor's office, and estimates are pooled across six Congresses and both parties. For Paul's systems, the paper is mainly a source of features and a set of caveats. No built component uses endorsement or group-signal data. The cosponsor forecaster has only member-dyad features, so bill-level outside-support signals are a possible addition. Any LDA-based substitute must respect D-021, however. The legislative pillar's efficiency term credits raw advancement rates without the majority-party adjustment that this paper's passage model shows matters. The solicitation ambiguity matches the system's finding that the lobbied-member link is circular.

works.title: LobbyView: Firm-level Lobbying & Congressional Bills Database
works.summary:
Kim's 2018 LobbyView note is a partial technical manual, not an empirical study. It has no estimates, no N and no stated coverage window. It documents how LDA lobbying reports get linked to congressional bills. First, a regex finds bill numbers. Then each mention is assigned to a Congress by taking the argmax of cosine similarity between the candidate bill text and the text around the mention, looking back three Congresses by default; if nothing matches, the code falls back to the filing-year Congress. The Congress is then propagated across the report by majority vote, titles are matched, and close bill numbers (gap of 10 or less) are expanded into ranges. Industries are grouped by NAICS2/SIC for per-industry Herfindahl indices, with Compustat merged in. The note names one failure case: Google's 2013 report cites H.R. 2577, which is a 112th-Congress bill, so the naive filing-year rule gets it wrong. It gives no error rates for any heuristic.

This matters for Paul's lobbying lane in three ways:
1. **Every LobbyView-derived member link is a bill-roster join, not a contact record.** That backs the system's finding that the lobbied-member link is circular.
2. **Paul's own LDA rebuild uses a different bill-resolution rule than the LobbyView pipeline.** A citation without an "of 20XX" suffix binds to the filing-year Congress, which is the naive rule this paper says fails. Hyphenated ranges are not expanded. So the network.csv vintage (2000-2022) and the 2021+ rebuild are different instruments with an unmeasured seam between them.
3. **The paper uses NAICS as an industry grouping.** The system has ruled NAICS to be linkage metadata only.

None of this is a validation of anything. The heuristics' accuracy is unreported, and the argmax always returns an answer.
works.question: No explicit research question. The document describes and documents the LobbyView database, which links congressional bill sponsorship with lobbying reports filed under the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995, and the API used to bulk-download it (Abstract; Section 1).
works.method: Descriptive data construction, not statistical estimation. Bills in reports are found by regular-expression search for bill numbers (Section 2, step 1). The Congress is assigned by maximizing the cosine similarity between a bag-of-words vector of each candidate bill and a vector of the text around the bill mention, over the candidate Congresses (Section 2, step 2, Eq. 1). Congress numbers propagate across a report, with majority vote where bills disagree (step 3). Bill titles are matched to report text (step 4). Bill ranges are expanded (step 5). Storage uses SQLite with SQLAlchemy and Elixir, and full-text search uses Whoosh over CRS summaries and specific issues (Sections 3.1, 5.4). Herfindahl indices are computed per industry (herfindahl.py), then augmented with a trade-issue indicator and Compustat data (herfindadd.py) (Section 5.5).

works.title: Bulk Ingestion of Congressional Actions and Materials Dataset (BICAM)
works.summary: BICAM (Delano, Rudkin and Kim, Scientific Data 2025) is a data descriptor, not a research article. It merges the Congress.gov and GovInfo APIs into one PostgreSQL/CSV release covering 421,764 bills (6th-119th Congress), 123,061 amendments, 2,597 members keyed by bioguide_id and icpsr, 226 committees and 587 subcommittees, 74,918 hearings, reports, prints, nominations and treaties. Its two external linkages are a bill crosswalk to Voteview and a Bill-to-LDA linkage that matches bill numbers and titles extracted from LD-2 Section 16 text to the Bills table by distance scores, with low-confidence matches reviewed by hand. The authors say this finds significantly more bill lobbying than earlier sources (Kim and Kunisky 2021), including ex-post lobbying. The main text gives no match counts, precision, recall or threshold; that material is in the Supplementary Information, which was not available here. Validation checks integrity only (completeness, types, unique keys, cross-source agreement) and treats Congress itself as ground truth. For Paul's system the paper matters at one point: how bill mentions in LD-2 filings are resolved. Melange's lobbying network uses its own parser for those mentions in build_network_2021_rebuild.py, which has a known 0.5 percent slash-citation loss, and then credits every sponsor and cosponsor of each lobbied bill. BICAM could be a second, independent path for checking bill resolution. It does not fix the circularity: the LDA still names bills, never the members contacted, so a bill-to-member join made from BICAM would still be P(joined given lobbied) = 1 by construction. Second, BICAM's bulk bills and cosponsors could replace or cross-check the congress.gov scrapers behind the activity score. That is a sourcing option and is UNVERIFIED until it is run.
works.question: No research question is posed. The paper's aim is to provide a standardized, linked, bulk-downloadable database of official U.S. congressional records (1789 to present) and to make Bill-to-LDA lobbying linkages available for interest-group research.
works.method: Data engineering rather than statistical analysis. Steps: (1) gather from both government APIs with a custom Python package (pause/resume, error recovery, parallel download); (2) import into PostgreSQL, enforce types and unique keys, and connect components by identifiers; (3) merge the two upstream sources with rules-based corrections, keeping the most complete composite record; (4) add record linkages to Voteview (custom bill identifier, crosswalk to Voteview) and to LDA Section 16 filings by matching extracted bill numbers and titles to Bills using distance measures, with low-confidence matches manually scrutinized.

works.title: Advancing the Empirical Research on Lobbying
works.summary: De Figueiredo and Richter (NBER WP 19698, 2013) is a narrative review with no new estimates. It sets out what the field agreed on about lobbying by 2013 and how to study it causally. The scale facts: federal lobbying was about 3.5 billion dollars in 2012, roughly five times interest-group campaign contributions. Corporations and trade associations account for over 84 percent of it. Only about 10 percent of public firms lobby, and a firm that lobbied last year lobbies this year with 92 percent probability. Its main argument is that lobbying panels are persistent, selected and confounded by unobserved channels. Fixed effects alone therefore cannot identify effects, and research should use exogenous shocks. The designs it reviews are difference-in-differences on legislator exits, event studies such as the Jeffords switch, cost-shifter instruments, Heckman selection, and structural all-pay contest models. It cites conditional returns: earmark gains only where the home legislator sits on Appropriations, a 1.07 percentage point lower tax rate per 1 percent more lobbying, and about 23 percent of lobbyist revenue lost when a former boss leaves office. It also notes that transaction (LDA) data record spending but not which legislator was targeted. For Paul's systems the essay mostly confirms choices already made. It agrees that the lobbied-member link is circular (LD-2 names no member) and explains why the sector-growth lobbying coefficient flips under year fixed effects. It also shows that the influence engine's money legs cover only PAC contributions, the smaller channel. Its shock-based designs point to tests the system has not run. Nothing in it argues for either rejected SNA proposal. Its revolving-door evidence must not be turned into influence language on staffer edges.
works.question: What empirical facts about lobbying are broadly agreed, what challenges block causal inference on lobbying effects, which quasi-experimental and structural methods can overcome them, and which data sources and open questions should drive the next generation of research (essay has no original estimates).
works.method: Narrative review and methods primer. Surveys the empirical facts on who lobbies, how much, and how it is organized (Sec II), then reviews five designs: difference-in-differences with exogenous shocks, event studies, instrumental variables (2SLS), two-step Heckman selection models, and structural modeling (Sec III.B). Also lists matching, regression discontinuity and synthetic control as untried for lobbying (p.29). Compares data classes: surveys, registries, transaction reports (Sec IV).
findings: Federal lobbying spending was about 3.5 billion dollars in 2012, against roughly 750 million a year in interest-group campaign contributions, about five times as large (Sec II.A, pp.5-6).
Corporations and trade associations account for over 84 percent of federal lobbying expenditures; issue-ideology membership groups about 2 percent (de Figueiredo 2004 as cited, Sec II.A, p.6).

Only about 10 percent of publicly traded firms lobby on their own behalf (Richter et al 2009; Kerr et al 2013); a firm lobbying last year lobbies this year with 92 percent probability (Sec II.A, p.7).
Budgeting periods are associated with a 19 percent increase in state interest-group lobbying expenditures across 38 states (de Figueiredo 2014; de Figueiredo and Cameron 2012) (Sec II.A, p.8).

Lobbyist revenue falls about 23 percent after the senator they formerly served is defeated or retires (Blanes i Vidal et al 2012) (Sec II.C, p.10); the essay attributes about 23 percent of lobbying services value to who you know (Sec III.B.1, p.20).

Richter et al (2009): a 1 percent increase in lobbying over baseline predicts a 1.07 percentage point lower effective tax rate in the next period, and the result survives a Heckman selection correction (Sec III.B.4, p.26).

works.title: Spillovers from regulating corporate campaign contributions
works.summary: Fremeth, Richter and Schaufele (MPRA working paper, 2018) ask whether the federal per-candidate cap on corporate PAC gifts (5,000 dollars per election, 10,000 per cycle) pushes firms into other political channels. They use S&P 500 firms with PACs, 1992-2008 FEC data (6.8M firm-candidate-cycle rows) and LDA lobbying for 2000-2008 (about 2,800 firm-cycles). Within a firm-cycle, a candidate who receives the PAC maximum is 6.6 points more likely to also receive a gift from the firm's CEO (Table 2), about 110 dollars more on average. Firms whose PAC maxes out any candidate spend about 549,000 dollars more on lobbying per cycle, with firm and industry-by-cycle fixed effects. A one-sided regression discontinuity at the limit gives jumps of 1.6M to 3.0M dollars, but the authors call its frictions assumption strong. Placebo outcomes (R&D, advertising, dividends, acquisitions) show no jump. The authors say no exogenous variation in the limit exists, so the estimates are partial correlations. Some numbers in the text do not match the tables. For Paul's systems, the paper bears mainly on how money is bounded. The Melange optimizer treats the 10,000-dollar PAC limit as the ceiling on CU spend per member, and the flip model counts competitor money only as bank and finserv PAC dollars. The paper suggests firms at the cap shift resources into executive giving and lobbying, which neither ledger sees. Mentat already tiers Chief-level employee giving by company, so a PAC-at-limit by Chief-giving join is a cheap extension. The paper's firm-level link between giving and lobbying does not contradict the member-level FEC-LDA bridge null. That bridge asks a different question, and the paper itself notes that LDA filings name no candidates.
works.question: Do statutory limits on corporate PAC campaign contributions generate spillover increases in other corporate political activity, namely CEO contributions to the same candidates and firm lobbying expenditures, at the regulated per-candidate contribution threshold?
works.method: Linear probability and OLS. CEO model (eq. 3, p.10): binary CEO-to-candidate contribution on PAC contributed and PAC at-limit indicators with firm-by-cycle and candidate-by-cycle fixed effects. Lobbying model (eq. 4, p.13): firm-cycle aggregate lobbying on PAC contributed and at-limit indicators with firm fixed effects and Fama-French 49 industry-by-cycle fixed effects. One-sided regression discontinuity (eq. 5, p.16): polynomial (linear or quadratic) in PAC dollars with a jump at the limit, with and without industry-cycle fixed effects. Difference-in-differences around BCRA (post-2003 cycle indicator, Table 6, p.18). Standard errors clustered by firm. Altonji, Elder and Taber (2005) selection-on-unobservables ratio reported for the main lobbying model (p.14).
findings: CEO supplementary giving (Table 2, p.28): at-limit PAC raises the probability a CEO gives to that candidate by 0.066 (SE 0.006). The text instead reports 7.7 percent (Section 4.1, p.11), a mismatch noted here.

CEO dollars (Table 2, p.28): at-limit PAC associated with 109.92 extra dollars (SE 10.05). Text reports 123 dollars (p.11); Table 7 (p.A-4) gives 123.88 (SE 10.55). Figure 2 shows 59.91 for the 4,500-4,999 bin versus the at-limit value.

Lobbying main estimate (Table 3 column 1, p.29; text p.14): firms whose PAC reaches the limit for any candidate spend 549,166 dollars more per cycle (SE 225,013; significant at 1 percent). Abstract gives a range of 549,000 to 1.6M dollars.
Lobbying firms only (Table 3 column 6, p.29; text p.15): at-limit coefficient 662,590 dollars (SE 305,066; significant at 5 percent).

Large-expenditure control (Table 3 columns 2-3, p.14-15): PAC-large-expenditure indicator is not significant; at-limit remains significant when both are included, about 250,000 dollars larger than the large-expenditure coefficient per text. Altonji-Elder-Taber ratio stated as 7.7 (p.14).

Placebo outcomes (Table 4, p.30; text p.15): at-limit coefficients are R&D 63.07 (SE 68.56), advertising 4.71 (SE 34.74), dividends -23.02 (SE 66.93), acquisitions 5.32 (SE 103.31); none significant. Units not stated in the paper.

works.title: The Dynamics of Firm Lobbying
works.summary: Kerr, Lincoln and Mishra (NBER WP 17577, Nov 2011; the AEJ: Economic Policy version is dated 2014) study why firm lobbying is so persistent. In a balanced Compustat panel of 3,260 US-headquartered public firms, 1998-2006, only 10 percent lobby in any year and 6.2 percent in a given year. Among firms that lobbied last year, 92 percent lobby again. In a typical year, 96 percent of lobbying dollars come from firms that lobbied the year before. The authors read this as evidence of sunk entry costs in a Roberts-Tybout model. A Blundell-Bond linear probability model puts the lagged-status effect at about 0.84-0.88. Within-firm fixed-effects OLS gives about 0.44, which the authors say is biased downward (Nickell). Entry clusters in the year before an election, not the election year itself, and exit does not follow the cycle. The policy test uses the 2004 lapse of the expanded H-1B cap. They interact each firm's 2001 dependence on foreign workers with a 2004-2006 dummy, with firm and year fixed effects, in 171 large patenting firms (846 core firm-years). Dependence raises lobbying on high-skill immigration (0.043, SE 0.014, LCA measure). It does not raise the chance of lobbying at all (-0.008, SE 0.009). No highly dependent non-lobbyist entered. All of the response came from firms that were already lobbying (the intensive margin). For Paul's systems this is mainly evidence about forecasting and specification. It backs Mentat's persistence-anchored lobbying forecasts, which leave out election-phase effects. It warns about the lagged-outcome lobbying equation with sector fixed effects in the sector growth study. It also shows that LDA reports cannot measure spending per issue, which is what the contested-bills question would need. The firm-level, 1998-2006 public-firm scope limits how far any of this transfers.
works.question: What determines the dynamics of firm lobbying over time? Do up-front entry costs explain the persistence of lobbying status, and how do firms respond to a policy shock (the 2004 expiry of the H-1B cap expansion) at the extensive versus intensive margin?
works.method: Reduced-form linear probability model of the lobbying indicator with lagged lobbying status and up to two lagged re-entry indicators (eq 2, p.10). Table 2: Blundell-Bond GMM (cols 2-6, lag-two instruments), OLS with state, industry and year FE (col 1), within firm-FE OLS (cols 7-8, Nickell bias acknowledged). Section 5: eq 3 interacts 2001 firm dependence (log LCA count, log Chinese and Indian patenting) with a 2004-2006 binding-cap dummy, with firm and year FE, clustered by firm. Table 4: cross-section, year FE. Table 6 uses always-lobbying firms (443 obs). Table 7 tabulates by quintile.
findings: Few firms lobby: 10 percent of 3,260 firms lobby in at least one year 1998-2006; 6.2 percent lobby in a given year (Table 1; intro p.2).
Persistence: P(lobby this year | lobbied last year) = 92 percent, above 80 percent in almost all two-digit NAICS industries (Sec 2, p.7).

Size gradient: lobbying firms average 5,407 vs 1,423 ($m) sales and 23k vs 7k employees for non-lobbying firms (Table 1); among lobbyists, correlation with spending is 28 percent for sales and 19 percent for employment (p.7).

Entry costs: lagged lobbying raises the probability of lobbying in the current year by about 88 percent in the baseline Blundell-Bond specification (text, p.10; Table 2 values 0.84-0.88 across cols 2-6). Within-FE and some other OLS values are smaller (recovered 0.44 and 0.34), but still significant per the text (p.12).
Concentration: in a typical year 96 percent of lobbying expenditure came from firms that lobbied the previous year (p.7).
Election timing: entry clusters in the year before an election, not the election year; exit is unrelated to the cycle (p.7).
